clue.text: Charming novel ?

parts.note: read as a book title, Walter Scott's crusader novel; read literally, an object that works as a charm

explanation.surface: A recommendation of a delightful new book.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Charming' looks like praise for the novel, but the clue means a thing that charms, and Scott wrote a novel with that very name.
explanation.definitionFit: A lucky charm or amulet is exactly this, and Walter Scott's 1825 novel of the Crusades bears the same title.

clue.text: Officer upset mine employees

indicators.note: in a down clue upset turns the word for mine upside down

parts.note: a pit is a mine
staff means employees

explanation.surface: An official overturns the work of a mine's employees.
explanation.walkthrough: 'upset' suggests annoyance, but in a down clue it turns PIT upwards to TIP.
explanation.definitionFit: A court official, such as a bailiff carrying a metal-tipped staff, holds this title.

clue.text: Lukewarm in religion, but converted Diana Cole

indicators.note: converted means changed into another form, so these letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: Diana Cole, once tepid about faith, has had a religious conversion.
explanation.walkthrough: The church at Laodicea is rebuked in Revelation for being neither hot nor cold.
explanation.definitionFit: From the church of Laodicea in Revelation, the word describes indifference or half-heartedness about faith.

clue.text: Rose's fruit appears on board in these vessels

definitions.text: Rose's fruit appears on board in these vessels

indicators.note: the fruit is placed inside the abbreviation for steamships

parts.note: SS stands for steamship, a kind of vessel
the fruit of the rose is the hip

explanation.surface: Rose hips are loaded aboard the cargo boats.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Rose' looks like a woman's name, but it is the flower, whose fruit are hips. HIPS sits inside SS, the abbreviation for steamship, and the whole clue describes ocean-going craft.
explanation.definitionFit: Large sea-going vessels; the hips are carried on board them.

clue.text: Settled about people obtaining food

indicators.note: the word for settled goes round the word for people

parts.note: alit means settled, as a bird alights
men means people

explanation.surface: Settlers bringing people provisions.
explanation.walkthrough: ALIT is an old past tense of alight, to come to rest.
explanation.definitionFit: A formal word for nourishment or sustenance.

clue.text: Shops put rent in duplicated quarterly letter

indicators.note: the torn word is placed in the middle of the doubled letter
duplicated says the compass letter is written twice over

parts.note: S (south) is one of the four compass quarters' letters
rent, as a past tense, means tore

explanation.surface: A shopkeeper slips the rent money into a letter sent every quarter.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Rent' is not money paid to a landlord but the past tense of rend. The compass points N, E, S, W are the 'quarterly' letters; S doubled holds TORE.
explanation.definitionFit: Shops and retail outlets are synonyms, as in department outlets.

clue.text: Endures a good deal putting up with poor Teresa

indicators.note: in a down clue putting up reverses the word for a good deal

parts.note: a lot means a good deal

indicators.note: poor here shows the name's letters are in bad shape and reordered

explanation.surface: Someone bears a great deal while putting up with unfortunate Teresa.
explanation.walkthrough: 'putting up with' reads as one phrase, but 'putting up' turns LOT to TOL and 'poor' rearranges TERESA to ERATES.
explanation.definitionFit: To bear or put up with something unpleasant is to endure it.

clue.text: School of the Lake District ?

parts.note: a school's name that is also a village and water in Cumbria

explanation.surface: Asking which school belongs to Cumbria's lakeland.
explanation.walkthrough: There is a school of this name in North Wales and a village by a lake in the Lake District, the hilly English region of Cumbria, where Wordsworth lived.
explanation.definitionFit: Rydal School is a school in Colwyn Bay, and Rydal is a Lake District village with its own water, home of Wordsworth's Rydal Mount.

clue.text: Able Punch editor ?

parts.note: a sailor's rank beginning Able, and the surname of an editor of the humorous magazine Punch

explanation.surface: A capable editor of a satirical weekly.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Able' looks like praise, but with this word it is the naval rank Able. Sir Owen Seaman edited Punch, the British humorous magazine, from 1906 to 1932.
explanation.definitionFit: An able-bodied rating in the navy holds this title, and Sir Owen of this surname edited the magazine Punch.

clue.text: Hostility is a problem in a rising

indicators.note: in a down clue rising reads the pieces from the bottom upwards

parts.note: a sum is an arithmetic problem

explanation.surface: Ill feeling becomes a difficulty during an uprising.
explanation.walkthrough: 'a rising' suggests a rebellion, but 'rising' turns SUM IN A upwards to ANIMUS.
explanation.definitionFit: Animosity or ill will towards someone is hostility.

clue.text: In favour of seeing the clause

parts.note: pro means for, in favour of
seeing, the faculty of sight, is vision

explanation.surface: Someone backing a contract term once they have read it.
explanation.definitionFit: A stipulation or condition in a legal document is called this.

clue.text: Miss Bennet has only half a day in Spain

indicators.note: only the second half of the word only is kept here

parts.note: the Spanish word for day is dia

explanation.surface: A Jane Austen heroine pays a fleeting visit to Spain.
explanation.walkthrough: 'only half' is wordplay: the latter half of ONLY gives LY. The Bennet sisters of Pride and Prejudice are Jane, Elizabeth, Mary, Kitty and the runaway youngest.
explanation.definitionFit: The youngest Bennet sister in Pride and Prejudice, who elopes with Wickham, has this first name.

clue.text: Ends the captain's call, perhaps ?

explanation.surface: Wrapping up after the captain calls at the coin toss.
explanation.walkthrough: Before a cricket match the captains toss a coin, and one calls heads or the other side.
explanation.definitionFit: The rear ends of animals or kites are their back parts; at a coin toss a captain may call the reverse side of the coin.

clue.text: Girl cooked dear meals

indicators.note: cooked means falsified or messed about, so these letters are reworked

explanation.surface: A young woman has prepared some lovely meals.
explanation.definitionFit: A woman's given name, borne by the gypsy dancer in Hugo's Hunchback of Notre-Dame.

clue.text: Load when about to go into combat

indicators.note: the short word for about is put into the word for combat

parts.note: combat means fight
re means about, concerning

explanation.surface: A soldier shouldering his pack before going into battle.
explanation.definitionFit: Cargo carried by ship, lorry or train is a load.

clue.text: Inexperienced Othello turns up in actors' place

parts.note: green means inexperienced

indicators.note: in a down clue turns up reverses the word for Othello

parts.note: Othello is the Moor of Venice in Shakespeare's play

explanation.surface: A novice actor playing Othello arrives at the theatre.
explanation.walkthrough: 'turns up' seems to mean arrives, but here it reverses MOOR to ROOM.
explanation.definitionFit: The room backstage where performers wait before going on is called this.

clue.text: Heavenly god of the rings

parts.note: a Roman deity whose name is also given to a planet circled by rings

explanation.surface: A deity in the heavens who rules over rings.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Heavenly' points both to an immortal and to a body in the sky; the planet is famous for its ring system.
explanation.definitionFit: The Roman god of sowing gave his name to the sixth planet, which has the most conspicuous rings.

clue.text: Place we get under way from

definitions.text: Place we get under way from

parts.words: Place we get under way from
parts.note: a sheltered stretch of water where ships lie at anchor before sailing

explanation.surface: Asking where a journey begins.
explanation.walkthrough: 'get under way' is the nautical phrase for a ship starting to move, so the place is an anchorage, not a starting line.
explanation.definitionFit: A sheltered offshore anchorage where ships ride before setting sail.

clue.text: Backs terribly sore between extremities

indicators.note: the scrambled letters sit between the parts of the word for extremities

parts.note: ends are extremities

indicators.note: terribly shows the word sore is badly mangled and rearranged

explanation.surface: A person with terribly sore hands and feet complains of back pain.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Backs' looks like a noun for body parts, but it is the verb, to support; 'terribly' is the anagram signal and 'between' the container one.
explanation.definitionFit: To support or approve a candidate or cheque is to back it.

clue.text: Order goods and leave some margin ?

explanation.surface: A clerk placing a supply order and leaving space at the edge of the page.
explanation.definitionFit: A requisition for supplies is an official order; setting text in from the edge leaves a blank margin.

clue.text: French historian rows round Holyhead

indicators.note: the word for rows goes round the single letter

parts.note: tiers are rows, as in seating
the head, or first letter, of Holy is H

explanation.surface: A French scholar rowing round the port of Holyhead.
explanation.walkthrough: Holyhead is a Welsh port, but the clue splits it as the head of 'Holy'.
explanation.definitionFit: Adolphe Thiers wrote histories of the French Revolution and later led the Third Republic.

clue.text: Mark follows us back — appears to keep up

indicators.note: the word for mark comes after the reversed piece
back says the word us is read the other way round

parts.note: a stain is a mark

explanation.surface: Someone noticing a mark trailing behind them that seems to persist.
explanation.definitionFit: To maintain or prolong something, such as a note or an effort, is to keep it going.

clue.text: British artist was worn out ?

explanation.surface: A British painter who has been wearing himself out.
explanation.walkthrough: Stanley Spencer was an English painter; a spencer is also a short jacket worn outdoors, so it 'was worn out' of doors.
explanation.definitionFit: Stanley Spencer painted Cookham scenes; the same name is given to a short jacket formerly worn outside over other clothes.

clue.text: Escapes from diva's love entanglement

indicators.note: entanglement shows the letters get mixed up together

parts.note: the word diva's supplies its letters with the s
love is zero in tennis, the letter O

explanation.surface: Someone getting away from an opera singer's romantic affair.
explanation.walkthrough: 'love entanglement' reads as an affair, but 'love' gives O and 'entanglement' scrambles it with DIVAS.
explanation.definitionFit: To dodge or steer clear of something is to escape it.

clue.text: Saint in mail ?

parts.note: a saint whose name is on a card sent through the post each February

explanation.surface: A holy man clad in chain mail.
explanation.walkthrough: 'mail' suggests armour, but it is the post, which carries cards named after the saint on 14 February.
explanation.definitionFit: A saint's day card sent anonymously to a sweetheart each 14 February carries his name.

clue.text: Some fool has advanced the capital-!

indicators.note: Some says the answer is a run of letters hidden inside the words that follow

parts.note: the letters run across the end of one word into the next

explanation.surface: A foolish person has put money into the capital.
explanation.walkthrough: 'advanced' suggests a loan of money, but it simply supplies its first letters to the run.
explanation.definitionFit: The capital of Tibet, seat of the Dalai Lama.

clue.text: Poet from East End backed mount

indicators.note: End points to the final letter of East
backed says the mountain's name is read backwards

parts.note: Ossa is a mountain in Greece

explanation.surface: A poet from London's East End climbs onto a horse that rears back.
explanation.walkthrough: 'East End' suggests London but gives the last letter of East, T. 'mount' looks like a horse; it is Mount Ossa in Thessaly, reversed to ASSO.
explanation.definitionFit: Torquato Tasso was an Italian Renaissance poet, author of Jerusalem Delivered.

clue.text: Essays in satire — not a new form

indicators.note: new form says the remaining letters take a different arrangement
not says the letter given by a is dropped

explanation.surface: Satirical essays that are not a new genre.
explanation.walkthrough: 'not a' removes A from SATIRE to leave STIRE, which 'new form' rearranges.
explanation.definitionFit: Attempts or efforts are essays in the old sense of the word.

clue.text: Girl appears to hail from this state

parts.note: Ida is a girl's name
ho is a call used to hail someone

explanation.surface: A young woman seems to come from somewhere particular.
explanation.definitionFit: A US state in the north-west, famous for potatoes.

clue.text: Those about to take service perhaps, in, some sets

definitions.text: Those about to take service perhaps

explanation.surface: Tennis players waiting to receive serve during several sets.
explanation.walkthrough: 'service' is a tennis serve and 'sets' are radio or television sets, not sets of a match.
explanation.definitionFit: Players returning serve in tennis are so called, and radios and television sets are also apparatus that pick up signals.

clue.text: Old musical instruments in first draft of "Major Barbara", perhaps?

parts.note: George Bernard Shaw wrote the play Major Barbara
a first draft is a manuscript, MS

explanation.surface: A theatrical archive holds an early handwritten version of a famous play.
explanation.walkthrough: Shaw's manuscript of his play would be SHAW + MS; 'perhaps' marks it as just one example.
explanation.definitionFit: Medieval double-reed woodwind instruments, ancestors of the oboe, go by this name.

clue.text: Takes chair with journalists, including one of foreign type

indicators.note: the word for journalists wraps round the other pieces

parts.note: the press means journalists collectively
I is the Roman numeral one
de is French for of, a foreign version of the word

explanation.surface: A chairperson takes the meeting alongside reporters, one of them from abroad.
explanation.definitionFit: To be in charge of a meeting as chairperson is to take the chair.
